newsitem.title: USA: Ohio to sue tobacco industry for health costs.
newsitem.headline: Ohio to sue tobacco industry for health costs.

text.p: Ohio will file suit next week against the tobacco industry, joining 24 other states that are seeking to recover public money spent treating smoking-related illnesses, the state's attorney general said Wednesday.

Ohio Attorney General Betty Montgomery said she was convinced by fellow attorneys general in a meeting on Monday in Chicago that Ohio's participation in the legal battle against the tobacco industry would be "pivotal."
With Ohio's entry, a majority of the 50 states will be suing the industry, Montgomery said in a statement. At least two other states were preparing lawsuits.
The attorneys general were set to renew negotiations with industry representatives next week in a bid to reach a ground-breaking industrywide settlement.

Sources close to the talks have indicated the tobacco companies may end up making payments of $300 billion over 25 years, in addition to curtailing marketing efforts while gaining some protection from future lawsuits.

Montgomery said Ohio's costs of treating smoking-related illnesses between 1980 and 1993 were estimated by the Centres for Disease Control at $3.3 billion. The Ohio Department of Health estimated that about 20,000 people die every year in the state from smoking-related illnesses.

Attorney General Mike Moore of Mississippi, which in 1995 became the first state to file suit against the industry to recover smoking-related Medicaid costs, said, "Attorney General Montgomery's timing couldn't have been better.

"Her decision gives our efforts a tremendous boost. Because of Ohio's influence nationally, and Betty Montgomery's bold action today, Ohio now has a seat at the table of these negotiations and can make a real difference," Moore said.

Montgomery said the state's lawsuit had been prepared in January but she had wanted to wait until Ohio's participation could "make a real difference." She said the state would also opt into the settlement with Liggett-Meyers in which the company agreed to share key documents and to pay a portion of its profits from cigarette sales.
Initially, state prosecutors will handle the suit, she said, but a national legal team was on stand-by to assist.
"Ohio is the only state suing the tobacco industry that has this type of innovative arrangement," Montgomery said.
